This verse opens with a rhetorical question that is meant to confirm a known fact: a long span of time passed over man during which he was nothing worth mentioning. The commentators differ on who "man" refers to. Qatada, al-Suddi and Ikrima, followed by al-Tabari, al-Mawardi and Ibn Kathir, take it to be Adam, while al-Zamakhshari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi understand the whole human species, a view also reported from Ibn 'Abbas and Ibn Jurayj. On the length of "that time", Ibn 'Abbas, through Abu Salih, gives forty years before the spirit was breathed in, while others count successive stages of clay, mud and dried clay. Some, as al-Mawardi and al-Razi report, say that the period has no fixed limit. The phrase "nothing worth mentioning" is read by al-Farra' and others as not yet existing or unidentified, and by Yahya ibn Salam as having no rank in creation.

For the "mingled drop", most commentators understand the mixing of the man's fluid and the woman's, a view held by Ibn 'Abbas, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir. Ibn Mas'ud took it to mean the veins within the drop, Mujahid and al-Dahhak the variety of its colours, and Qatada the successive stages of formation from drop to clot to lump of flesh. Al-Tabari prefers the first reading. The phrase "We test him" is explained as testing through commands and prohibitions, through good and evil fortune, or through gratitude in ease and patience in hardship. Making him hearing and seeing is described as a favour and a proof, and al-Tabari adds that the trial also presupposes sound reason.

Finally, "We guided him to the way, whether grateful or ungrateful" means that he was shown the paths of good and evil, as Ikrima, 'Ata', Ibn Zayd and Mujahid explain, while al-Suddi and al-Dahhak take the way to be his exit from the womb. The construction "either... or" is also debated: the Kufans treat the particle as a conditional with an added element, which the Basrans reject.

The commentators explain that this verse recalls the origin of the human being: God created him from a mixed drop, made of the fluid of the man and of the woman, then gave him hearing and sight so that he might be tested through responsibility, and showed him the path of good and evil, so that he becomes either grateful or ungrateful. Most agree that 'man' here means the whole human species and that 'amshaj' means mixtures. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Qurtubi report that this is the mingling of the man's and the woman's fluids in the womb, a view supported by Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, al-Hasan and al-Rabi'. Al-Tabari judges it the most sound, since a drop that has become a clot is no longer a drop. Ibn Mas'ud takes the term to mean the veins within the drop, al-Dahhak and Mujahid take it to mean the different colours of the drop, and Qatada means the successive stages of formation. Al-Hasan, cited by al-Baghawi and al-Zamakhshari, links it to menstrual blood. As for the trial, most understand it as a test through command and prohibition, and good and evil, while al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Atiyya also take it as the transfer from one state to another. The commentators present these views without deciding between them.

This verse states that God guided the human being to the path, and that he then becomes either grateful (shakir) or ungrateful (kafur). Al-Tabari explains that the verse means God made the path to Paradise clear to him, whether he chooses gratitude or disbelief; he notes that "imma" may function as a conditional or as "or", and reports that a grammarian of Basra took the phrase as a clause describing the pronoun in "hadaynahu". Mujahid understands the path as the way to misery and happiness, while Qatada links gratitude and ingratitude to God's blessings. Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi, al-Qurtubi and most exegetes take the guidance as a clarification of the two ways, leaving the choice to the person. Al-Razi lists several grammatical readings and notes that the Ash'aris see here the affirmation that God creates good and evil, a view the Mu'tazilites reject. Ibn 'Ashur sees a division according to people's condition when the message came. Al-Zamakhshari cites a reading of Abu al-Sammal with an open hamza, which he takes to mean that the grateful receive divine success and the ungrateful bear their poor choice. The commentators agree that gratitude and ingratitude are two states of the human being, but they differ over the nature of guidance and the role of divine decree. No legal ruling is drawn from this verse.

This verse states that God has prepared for the disbelievers chains with which they will be dragged, shackles that bind their hands to their necks, and a blazing fire. It follows the statement that man was guided to the path, and that he will be either grateful or ungrateful. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi explain that the shackles bind the hands to the neck, and that the chains are used to drag the condemned. Al-Qurtubi and al-Baghawi add that each chain is seventy cubits long, citing another passage of the Quran. The word sa'ir means a fire kindled and stoked. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Razi note that the mention of these punishments is meant to instil fear. On the meaning of gratitude and ingratitude, Mujahid and Muqatil take them to mean happiness and wretchedness, while Qatada takes them to mean thankfulness for God's blessings or denial of them. On recitation, the readers of Medina, al-Kisa'i and Abu Bakr on the authority of 'Asim read salasila with tanwin, while others read it without, since the word is normally not declined. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya explain the tanwin either as a replacement for the final long vowel or as a usage found among some Arabs who decline such words. Abu 'Ubayd prefers tanwin in order to follow the written text of the Quran. The commentators do not decide between these readings and simply record them as accepted variants.

This verse says that the righteous, meaning sincere and obedient believers, will drink in the Hereafter from a cup whose drink is mixed with camphor. The commentators differ on what the camphor is. Al-Kalbi, Ata', Ibn Kaysan, Mujahid and al-Farra' hold that it is the name of a spring in Paradise whose water is mixed into the drink, a view al-Tabari also reports and which Ibn Kathir presents as the most common reading. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Ikrima take it to refer to the taste, the scent or the coldness of the drink, and the grammarians say the drink is like camphor in whiteness, fragrance and coolness, since camphor is not drunk. Muqatil, according to al-Mawardi, identifies the spring with tasnim. Ibn Atiyya judges the preposition 'bi' to be superfluous, while others keep it in the sense of joining. The phrase 'yufajjirunaha tafjiran' is explained by al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir as the believers' ability to channel the water wherever they wish, through their homes and palaces. Some commentators also note that the 'cup' may mean the vessel or the wine itself. The commentators agree that this passage describes a reward for faithful believers, set in contrast with the fate of the disbelievers just before. The general meaning is a divine favour granted to the righteous: a pleasant, refreshing drink, whose details belong to revelation.

This verse speaks of the righteous, the sincere believers who obey their Lord, who will drink in Paradise from a cup mixed with camphor, valued for its coolness, whiteness and fragrance, from a spring that the servants of God drink from and make flow wherever they wish from their homes and palaces, with ease. Al-Hasan, Qatada and Mujahid said the drink is mixed with camphor and sealed with musk, while Ikrima took the mizaj to mean its taste, and Ibn Kaysan spoke of a scent perfumed with camphor, musk and ginger. Muqatil held that it is not the camphor of this world, but that God names what is in Paradise by what people know. As for the spring, al-Farra' and al-Kalbi said that it is itself called camphor, or a spring of that name, while al-Zajjaj preferred to read it as drinking from a spring. Scholars differ on the sense of the preposition 'bi': al-Farra' takes it as meaning to quench oneself, al-Asma'i and Ibn Qutayba as meaning 'from', and Ibn al-Qayyim, reasoning grammatically, reads it as an implied verb of quenching. Mujahid and Qatada explain that the spring follows its drinkers wherever they turn. Muqatil identifies it with tasnim, the noblest drink of Paradise, and some report that it flows toward the dwellings of the prophets and believers. On the name 'righteous', Ibn 'Umar relates it to their kindness to parents and children, al-Hasan to their not harming anyone, and Qatada to their fulfilling God's rights. Commentators also record reports on the occasion of revelation, some attributed to 'Ali and Fatima, which Ibn Kathir and others regard as weak.

The seventh verse of Surat al-Insan describes the righteous in this world: they fulfil the vows they have made to God and fear a Day whose evil is widespread and far-reaching. The commentators differ on what a vow means. Qatada takes it to mean the duties God has enjoined, such as prayer, zakat, fasting and pilgrimage, while Mujahid and Ikrima understand vows made in obedience to God, al-Kalbi speaks of covenants, and Malik takes it as an obligation the person binds upon himself. As for the word mustatir, Ibn Abbas explains it as spreading and pervasive, al-Farra and al-Kalbi as stretched out and prolonged, and Qatada says the evil of that Day fills the heavens and the earth. Muqatil details it: the sky splits, the stars scatter, the mountains are crushed. Al-Razi observes that the fear mentioned is a matter of intention, which completes the act, so the verse joins deed and inner purpose. The scholars agree in praising faithfulness without deciding between the meanings of the terms. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi note that the present tense signals continuity, and that fulfilling a vow stands by implication for fulfilling all obligations, since whoever keeps what he has bound himself to will keep even more faithfully what God has bound him to.

This verse describes the conduct of the righteous in this world: they feed the needy even though they love food and need it themselves, giving to the poor man unable to earn his living, the orphan who has lost his father and has no property, and the captive. Mujahid, Ibn Jubayr and 'Ata' take the captive to be a Muslim prisoner held rightfully; Qatada and Ibn 'Abbas, followed by al-Hasan, understand a polytheist prisoner; 'Ikrima understands a slave; Abu Sa'id al-Khudri includes both the slave and the imprisoned; Abu Hamza al-Thumali understands a woman. Al-Tabari holds that the word is general and covers both kinds of captives, Muslim and polytheist. Sa'id ibn Jubayr says the command to feed a polytheist captive was abrogated by the verse of the sword, while others hold it remains valid, with feeding the orphan and the poor being voluntary charity. The righteous say, aloud or within themselves, that they feed for the sake of God, seeking neither reward nor thanks; Mujahid notes they did not say it, but God knew it in their hearts and praised them for it. They fear a day whose evil spreads far; Ibn 'Abbas explains the stern face as the drawing together of the features under the weight of that day. Narratives linking the verse to 'Ali and Fatima are judged weak or fabricated by al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur, who keep a general application.

This verse describes the righteous who drink from a cup mixed with camphor, who fulfil their vows and fear a day whose evil spreads far and wide. They feed the poor, the orphan and the captive although they love food and need it. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir read this as giving while in a state of desire for the food, while Ibn al-Jawzi and Ibn Juzayy allow that the pronoun may refer to God or to the food, preferring the latter. Commentators differ on the captive: Ibn Abbas, Qatada and al-Hasan take him to be a polytheist prisoner, Mujahid, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and 'Ata a Muslim held in lawful custody, 'Ikrima a slave, and Abu Hamza al-Thumali a woman. Al-Tabari holds the term general, covering all of these, and Ibn Kathir notes that the prisoners of that time were mostly polytheists. Al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi report that they say, verbally or in intention, that they seek no reward or thanks. Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr add that they did not say it aloud but God knew it in their hearts. The report that the sura concerns 'Ali and Fatima is judged weak or fabricated by Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur. Al-Razi observes that the giving counts only when sincerely meant for God. Most read shukur as a verbal noun like shukr, al-Zamakhshari as a pattern of infinitive, and al-Qurtubi as a general term.

This verse describes the righteous, who feed the poor, the orphan and the captive although they love food and need it themselves. They say, within themselves or aloud depending on the commentators, that they seek neither reward nor thanks, and that they fear from their Lord a day that is grim and bitter. The exegetes give several meanings to the two terms. Ibn 'Abbas, 'Ikrima, Sa'id ibn Jubayr and Qatada explain that faces will scowl that day, and that a disbeliever will sweat something like tar between his eyes. Ibn 'Abbas also explains that 'abus' means constricted and 'qamtarir' means long, while al-Kalbi, al-Akhfash and Ibn Zayd take it to mean severe and hard, and al-Zajjaj links the word to a she-camel drawing in her tail. Most hold that calling the day 'grim' is a metaphor, either transferring to the day the character of its people or comparing it to a scowling lion. Nearly all agree that God preserves them from the evil of that day, gives them radiance on their faces and joy in their hearts, and rewards their patience with a garden and silk. The word 'captive' is disputed: Ibn 'Abbas, Qatada, al-Hasan, Mujahid and Sa'id ibn Jubayr understand a polytheist prisoner, a believer imprisoned or a detainee, 'Ikrima a slave, and Abu Hamza al-Thumali a woman. Some hold that the duty toward polytheist captives was abrogated by the verse of the sword, others that it remains in force. As for the occasion of revelation, several accounts exist, notably the one attributed to Ibn 'Abbas about Ali, Fatima and their sons, and the one reported by Muqatil about a man of the Ansar. Ibn 'Ashur judges the accounts concerning Ali and Fatima weak, and many commentators did not adopt them.

The commentators explain that God protected the righteous from the evil of that dreadful day which they feared, and gave them radiance in their faces and joy in their hearts as a reward for their patience. They differ on the meaning of "nadra": al-Dahhak takes it as whiteness and purity, Ibn Jubayr as beauty and brightness, and Ibn Zayd as the trace of blessing. As for the day, Ibn Abbas explains "ʿabūs" as constricted and "qamṭarīr" as long, while Qatada, Mujahid and Muqatil read it as the day that contracts faces and brows through its severity, and al-Kalbi and Ibn Zayd as harsh and grim. Ibn Kathir and al-Tabari consider Ibn Abbas's explanation the clearest, since the word describes what is very hard and burdensome.

The commentators agree that the reward was given for their patience in obedience and in abstaining from sin, though they differ on what this patience covered: hunger according to Ibn Abbas and Ata', poverty according to al-Dahhak. Al-Baghawi and al-Samʿani relate that al-Hasan said God admitted them to Paradise and clothed them in silk. Al-Zamakhshari notes that mentioning silk alongside Paradise points to the ease of life and the splendour of their dwelling and dress.

Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Tabari report that these verses were revealed about the generosity of ʿAlī, Fatima and their children towards the needy. Al-Razi, however, holds that the verses speak generally of all the righteous without singling out one person, although those named are included. Ibn Kathir takes the captive mentioned to be a polytheist captive, while al-Mawardi reports other opinions about who is meant.

This verse from Surat al-Insan describes the reward of the righteous for their patience. The commentators explain that God protected them from the evil of that grim, harrowing day, gave them radiance in their faces and joy in their hearts, and then rewarded their patience with a garden and silk. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and Ibn al-Jawzi understand this patience as steadfastness in obeying God and in refraining from disobedience. Ibn 'Abbas and Qatada also count patience under trials, while Dahhak links it to poverty, 'Ata' to hunger, and al-Qurtubi to fasting. Al-Baghawi and Ibn 'Atiyya describe the garden as an orchard with pleasant food, and the silk as fine dress. Al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi argue that pairing silk with the garden points to a mild climate, with neither a scorching sun nor a biting cold. Mujahid and Qatada take zamharir to mean intense cold, whereas Tha'lab reports that in the dialect of Tayy it means the moon. The righteous recline on couches in canopied alcoves, and the shade of the trees hangs low over them while their fruit is brought within easy reach, according to Ibn Kathir and al-Zamakhshari. Accounts of the occasion of revelation differ. Some attribute it to Mut'im ibn Waraqa al-Ansari, others to 'Ali, Fatima and their children. Ibn Kathir, al-Tha'alibi and Ibn 'Ashur regard the latter story as weakly transmitted, and the commentators do not settle between these reports.

This passage describes the reward of the righteous in Paradise. The commentators explain that they will recline on couches, the arā'ik, which they take to be beds set within canopied enclosures; according to Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and al-Baghawi, a couch is only called arīka when it stands inside a canopy. The verse adds that they will see in Paradise neither a sun whose heat would harm them nor zamharīr. All agree that its air is temperate. On zamharīr, al-Tabari, Mujahid and Ibn Kathir take it to mean intense cold, while Ibn Mas'ud describes it as a kind of punishment, and Tha'lab, as cited by al-Razi, al-Qurtubi and al-Alusi, identifies it with the moon in the dialect of the Tayy tribe. On this second reading Paradise shines with its own light and needs neither sun nor moon. Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and al-Baydawi report that the shade of the trees will be close to its people and that the fruit will lower itself to whoever reaches for it, whether standing, sitting or lying down, according to Mujahid and Qatada. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Ashur explain that the reward is tied to the patience shown in this world. No legal ruling is drawn from this passage in the commentaries cited.

This verse describes the comfort of the righteous in Paradise. Reclining on couches, they see neither the scorching sun nor bitter cold, the shade of the trees is close above them, and their fruits hang low so they can pick them standing, sitting or lying down. The commentators read the word “daniya” as describing the shade drawing near, and they differ on its grammar: al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Nasafi take it as a circumstantial phrase linked to “reclining”, al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi offer several readings, and some hold it to be an attribute of a Paradise mentioned before. Mujahid explains the subduing of the fruit as its bending to whoever wishes to take it, while al-Mawardi adds the possibility that the fruit is freed from its sheaths and stones. There is broad agreement that the vessels of silver have the whiteness of silver and the clarity of glass, and that the cups have no handles, and that their measure matches each drinker's thirst. Ibn Abbas and Qatada take the zanjabil to be a spring in Paradise, whereas others take it as a flavour added to the drink. Al-Tabari and al-Qurtubi cite the view that the mukhalladun are youths who never age, while Abu 'Ubayda reads the word as meaning youths adorned with earrings. Ibn Kathir and Ibn 'Ashur stress the vastness of the kingdom given to the people of Paradise.

This passage describes the drink served to the people of Paradise in precious vessels: silver flagons and cups (akwab, the handleless, spoutless drinking vessels) are passed around them. The commentators agree that the glasses are made of silver yet have the clarity of glass, so they are not ordinary glass. Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid, al-Sha'bi and Qatada report that the soil of Paradise is silver and that its vessels are made from it. Ibn 'Abbas adds that if silver of this world were hammered until it was as thin as a fly's wing, the water behind it would still be visible, whereas the glasses of Paradise combine silver's whiteness with the transparency of glass.

On the phrase "qaddarûhâ taqdîrâ", most exegetes, including Ibn Kathir, Ibn 'Abbas, Mujahid and Qatada, understand that the vessels are measured exactly to each drinker's thirst, neither overflowing nor falling short. Al-Rabi' took this to mean the size of a palm, while al-Hasan held that the drinkers themselves determined the measure in their minds and the vessel came to match it. Ibn al-Qayyim considers the majority view the most eloquent.

The drink is mixed with ginger (zanjabil), which the Arabs prized. Mujahid says zanjabil is the name of the spring from which the righteous drink; Qatada says the near ones drink it pure and it is mixed for the rest. Concerning "salsabil", Ikrima takes it as the name of the spring, Mujahid describes it as a water that flows smoothly, and Qatada as a tractable stream that they direct as they wish; most commentators treat the word as a description meaning exceptionally smooth to swallow. As for the immortal youths, Qatada says they never die, al-Hasan and al-Dahhak say they are children who never grow older, and Ibn 'Abbas says they are adorned with earrings; their appearance is likened to scattered pearls.

This verse describes the vessels of Paradise as crystal-clear glass made of silver, combining the whiteness of silver with the transparency of glass so that what is inside can be seen from outside. The commentators agree on this image, which has no equal in this world. Ibn 'Abbas and al-Kalbi add that the earth of Paradise is silver and that these vessels are made from it. On the phrase 'they measured it with a measure', opinions differ about who did the measuring. Al-Hasan holds that the drinkers measured them in their own minds, so that they came out as they wished. Mujahid, Ibn Zayd and Qatada say they were fitted to the amount needed to quench thirst, neither overflowing nor falling short. Ibn 'Abbas, al-Rabi' and al-Dahhak say they were sized to the hand, and al-Sha'bi says they were measured for the drinkers with neither surplus nor deficit. Ibn Kathir and al-Sa'di consider these views compatible, since the cups fit both thirst and the hand. The drink is mixed with ginger; Mujahid and Qatada understand Zanjabil as the name of a spring in Paradise, while others take it as a flavour. The spring called Salsabil is named for its smoothness and easy passage down the throat, and most exegetes treat the word as an adjective rather than a proper name.

This verse describes the drink that the righteous will be given in Paradise: a cup whose mixture is ginger. The commentators explain that the drink is blended with ginger, a flavour the Arabs found especially pleasant for its sharp, agreeable taste. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi, Ibn Kathir, al-Qurtubi and Abu Hayyan report this meaning. Ibn Kathir adds that the righteous sometimes receive a drink mixed with camphor and at other times with ginger, so that the two balance each other, while those brought near to God drink it unmixed, according to Qatada. Mujahid held that zanjabil is the name of a spring from which the drink of the righteous comes, and Qatada described it as a smooth spring. Al-Razi, al-Zamakhshari and Ibn Juzayy also note that the taste is pleasant without the sting of ginger. As for the spring called salsabil, most scholars, including al-Tabari and al-Zajjaj, understood it as a descriptive word meaning very smooth water that slides easily down the throat, rather than a proper name. Mujahid described it as a spring that flows swiftly, and others said it flows freely wherever its drinkers wish. Ibn al-Qayyim observes that most scholars treat it as an adjective, without going further into the exact nature of the spring.

This verse describes the drink of the people of Paradise, mixed with ginger, and a spring called salsabil. The commentators agree that the root of the word denotes smoothness and ease of passage down the throat, and that the water is sweet and pleasant. Al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that Qatada described it as a smooth, obedient spring that its inhabitants guide wherever they wish, while Mujahid described it as having a swift flow. Al-Zamakhshari and Ibn 'Atiyya note that the Arabs liked ginger in their drinks and used it to describe the taste of a woman's mouth. On the ginger itself, Mujahid and Qatada take it to be the name of a spring from which those brought near drink pure while the rest of the people drink it mixed, others take it to be simply a taste found in the water, and Muqatil says it does not resemble the ginger of this world. Most exegetes, including al-Tabari, al-Zajjaj and al-Baghawi, treat salsabil as a descriptive adjective rather than a proper name, while al-Razi and Ibn al-Jawzi allow that it may be a name. Some read it as an imperative to seek a path, but al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan reject this reading, which al-Zamakhshari attributes to Ali while judging it strained.

In this verse God describes the youths who move among the people of Paradise to serve them. He calls them mukhalladun, meaning that they remain as they are, neither aging nor dying, and when one sees them one takes them for scattered pearls, because of their beauty, the brightness of their faces and their large number as they move about serving. The commentators agree on the idea of a permanent youth and beauty, but differ on the exact sense of the word. Qatada and Ibn Kathir understand it as immortality or unchanging state, while al-Hasan and al-Dahhak take it to mean children who do not grow up and youths who do not age. Ibn al-Jawzi, Ibn al-Qayyim and others report that in the Himyarite dialect it means those adorned with earrings, a view attributed to Abu 'Ubayda, Ibn al-A'rabi and Sa'id ibn Jubayr and supported by a line of poetry. Most read the image of scattered pearls as abundance and splendour, and al-Razi and al-Nasafi note that scattered pearls are more striking to the eye than strung ones. On who these youths are, 'Ali and al-Hasan al-Basri hold that they are the children of believers who died young, others that they are the children of polytheists, and Ibn al-Qayyim leans toward beings created by God in Paradise. As for the following phrase, most explain the great kingdom as the vastness of the dwellings, al-Suddi, al-Kalbi and Muqatil as the angels asking permission before entering, and Ibn 'Umar reports that the least-ranked inhabitant of Paradise surveys a realm extending two thousand years' journey.

This passage of Surat al-Insan describes what the people of Paradise see and the blessings that surround them. God tells His Prophet ﷺ that wherever he looks in Paradise he will see a bliss beyond description and a vast, great dominion. The commentators agree that the bliss refers to the comfortable life enjoyed by the people of Paradise, and that the eternal young servants who attend them remain in the appearance of youths who neither age nor change; their likening to scattered pearls refers to their whiteness, beauty and large numbers as they move about serving. Qatada holds that they do not die, while al-Dahhak and al-Hasan say they stay young without growing up, and Ibn Abbas says they are adorned with bracelets, others that they wear earrings. As for the great dominion, Sufyan al-Thawri, Mujahid, al-Kalbi and Muqatil take it to be the angels asking permission to enter upon the believers and greeting them; others understand it as vast sovereignty, reporting that the least-ranked of the people of Paradise looks over a kingdom spanning two thousand years, and others as a kingship that never ends. Some exegetes held that the verb 'see' has no stated object so that the sight extends to everything seen there; al-Farra' proposed an implied object, which al-Zajjaj rejected. Readers differ on the vocalization of 'aliyahum' and grammarians discuss its parsing. Ibn Kathir notes that whoever reflects on the gift given to the least-ranked of Paradise will understand what awaits the highest in rank.

This verse describes the adornment and drink of the righteous in Paradise: they wear green garments of fine silk (sundus) and thick silk (istabraq), are adorned with silver bracelets, and their Lord gives them a pure drink. The commentators agree on the general meaning: this is a reward and an honour for the righteous. The readings differ over the grammar of 'aliyahum', 'khudr' and 'istabraq'. Abu 'Ubayd and Abu Hatim prefer reading 'khudr' in the nominative and 'istabraq' in the genitive; Ibn 'Atiyya and Abu Hayyan note other possibilities, and az-Zamakhshari treats 'aliyahum' as an adverb of place or a circumstantial state. Ibn Kathir states that both fabrics are silk. On the bracelets, al-Razi and as-Suyuti explain that they may be of gold or silver, alternately or together, and Sa'id ibn al-Musayyab mentions three bracelets, of silver, gold and pearls. As for the pure drink, Abu Qilaba, an-Nakha'i and Ibrahim at-Taymi say it does not turn into urine but into a sweat smelling like musk, while Muqatil describes a spring at the gate of Paradise that removes rancour and envy from the heart. Al-Razi and al-Qurtubi note that 'tahur' here means perfect purity. The commentators see in this gift a special honour, since God Himself gives them to drink.

This verse tells the righteous that the bliss just described is their reward for their deeds in this world, and that their striving was "thanked", meaning accepted and rewarded. The commentators differ on who is addressed. Some take it as said to the blessed when they enter Paradise, others as a divine statement about what has been prepared for them. Qatada explains that God forgave their sins and accepted their good deeds, while Ata' says that God thanked them by giving them the best reward. Al-Razi lists several ways to understand God's "thanks": God is pleased with a small effort and gives much in return, or God is satisfied with his servants. The next verse, which tells the Prophet to be patient and not to obey the sinner or the disbeliever, is read by al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir as referring to Abu Jahl, while Muqatil names 'Utba ibn Rabi'a and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira. Ibn 'Atiyya and al-Tabari note that "aw" can mean "and", so the sense covers anyone of that kind. As for the command to remember the Lord "morning and evening", some take it as the five prayers, others as general remembrance, and Ibn Zayd holds that any obligation was abrogated. Several commentators relate reports about the occasion of revelation, such as the story of 'Ali's family, but the central meaning of the verse remains reward and divine approval.

This passage states that God Himself sent down the Quran upon His Prophet Muhammad, peace be upon him, in stages, verse after verse rather than all at once, and orders him to be patient with his Lord's decree and not to obey any of the disbelievers who is sinful or ungrateful. The commentators see in it both a reassurance to the Prophet and a statement that the revelation comes from God alone, its gradual descent reflecting divine wisdom. Ibn Abbas, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Qurtubi take the sending down to mean that the Quran came piece by piece, while al-Zamakhshari and al-Razi explain that the repeated pronoun after the emphatic particle establishes that nothing about the revelation is arbitrary, and that delaying permission to fight was part of that wisdom. As for the two figures named, Qatada, al-Baghawi and Ibn Kathir report that the sinner refers to Abu Jahl, whereas Muqatil and others name Utba ibn Rabi'a and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who offered the Prophet wealth and marriage to abandon his message. Ibn Atiyya, Abu Hayyan and al-Zamakhshari prefer to read the phrase as general, covering any sinner or disbeliever, and al-Farra and Abu Ubayda take the word "or" to mean "and", while al-Zajjaj holds that each of the two is deserving of disobedience. Some scholars consider the command to patience abrogated by the verse of the sword, a view others reject, and the commentators do not settle the matter.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to be patient with the decree of his Lord, that is, with God's decision to delay victory over the idolaters and with the burdens of conveying the message and bearing the harm it brings, and forbids him to obey any of them, whether a sinner (athim), meaning one who commits transgressions, or an ingrate (kafur), meaning one who denies blessings and persists in disbelief. The commentators agree that the target is the Quraysh offers of wealth, marriage or leadership in return for abandoning the call, and that forbidding obedience to either one implies forbidding obedience to both together. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir explain the sinner as one who commits sins and the ingrate as one who denies in the heart, while al-Zamakhshari reads the 'aw' as indicating a division of types, and al-Farra' takes it to mean 'and'. Qatada and al-Tabari report that the verse was sent down about Abu Jahl, who threatened to trample the Prophet's neck if he saw him pray; Muqatil, al-Baghawi and others name 'Utba ibn Rabi'a and al-Walid ibn al-Mughira, who offered a wife and money respectively. Al-Razi holds that the terms are general and not tied to one person. The commentators also agree that the verse goes on to command remembrance of God's name at morning, evening and part of the night, though they differ on the details: some identify the five prayers, others see a recommended practice, and Ibn Zayd considers the command abrogated. The following verses describe those who love the fleeting present and neglect the heavy Day, remind that God created them and can replace them, and state that the Qur'an is a reminder whose guidance rests on God's will.

God commands His Prophet in this verse to remember the name of his Lord at dawn and at dusk. The commentators differ on what this remembrance means. Several, among them Ibn 'Abbas, Ibn Zayd and Ibn Habib, take it as a reference to the five daily prayers: the dawn prayer corresponds to 'bukra', the midday and afternoon prayers to 'asil', and the sunset and night prayers to the portion of the night. Others understand it as a general remembrance and glorification of God, both in prayer and outside it. Al-Razi and Ibn Kathir favour the broader sense, describing a constant invocation at every hour. Al-Mawardi and al-Nasafi keep the liturgical reading, while Ibn Juzayy and Abu al-Su'ud treat it as a general command.

The night worship is also debated. The command to prostrate and glorify Him for a long part of the night is read by al-Baghawi and al-Mawardi as voluntary night prayer, the tahajjud. Ibn Habib sees it as a recommendation, while Ibn Zayd and others hold that it was abrogated by the five daily prayers. Some scholars, as al-Shawkani reports, consider it specific to the Prophet. Al-Qurtubi and Ibn 'Ashur note that the word 'min' here indicates a part of the night.

The commentators connect the verse to what precedes it: the Prophet should rely on prayer and remembrance to endure the hostility of the Meccan unbelievers. Al-Biqa'i and al-Tabari also link the passage to the prohibition of obeying the sinner or the disbeliever. Ibn 'Ashur concludes that devotion is a support that helps him persevere in his call.

In this verse God commands His Prophet ﷺ to prostrate to Him and to glorify Him during part of the night, keeping vigil for a long stretch. Most commentators understand the glorification as prayer. Al-Tabari, citing Ibn 'Abbas, explains that it means prayer and a long night vigil, and he reports that Ibn Zayd considered it an obligation at first, later abrogated. Al-Baghawi and Ibn al-Jawzi take the prostration to mean the sunset and night prayers, and the glorification to mean the voluntary prayer after the obligatory one. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi relate the view of Ibn Habib that the verse covers the five daily prayers, while others consider it a recommendation or a rule specific to the Prophet. Ibn Kathir links this passage to Surah Al-Muzzammil and Surah Al-Isra and sees it as a help in bearing the insults of the disbelievers. Ibn 'Ashur notes that the night is a time of withdrawal from preaching. Al-Zamakhshari reads the particle min as partitive, the long night being two-thirds, half, or a third of it. Al-Qasimi and others stress how strongly the Qur'an encourages night vigil.

This verse describes people who love the hasty life of this world and leave behind them a heavy day, which most commentators identify as the Day of Resurrection, a day they neglect and do not prepare for. Al-Tabari notes that 'wara'ahum' ordinarily means 'behind them', in the sense of abandoning something, though some read it as 'before them'; he judges the first meaning closer to the word's usage, and al-Sam'ani and al-Zamakhshari likewise understand the phrase as neglect of the Hereafter.

The commentators agree that calling the day heavy is a figure for its severity and terror. Al-Sam'ani gives two readings: its dread is great, or the judgment passed there between the servants weighs heavily on the wrongdoers. Ibn 'Atiyya explains that the heaviness falls on the disbelievers, as sleep weighs on one who sleeps.

They differ over who is meant. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn speak of the polytheists of Mecca. Al-Mawardi and al-Qurtubi also mention, as possibilities, the Jews who concealed the Prophet's description, or the hypocrites whose love of worldly gain betrays their hidden disbelief. Al-Mawardi suggests that for the Jews the heavy day may be killing and exile, and for the hypocrites it is the Day of Judgment.

Al-Razi argues that their motive is not doubt but love of immediate pleasures, while Ibn al-Qayyim links the verse to standing before God in prayer, saying that whoever stands well there will find that day lighter.

The commentators explain that this verse reminds of God's power over creation and resurrection: He created humankind and firmly fashioned its frame, and if He wills, He can destroy these deniers and replace them with others of their kind, but obedient. The scholars differ on the meaning of "asr". Ibn Abbas, Mujahid, Qatada and Muqatil take it to mean the physical makeup and form, a view that al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir prefer; Abu Hurayra, al-Hasan and al-Rabi' take it to mean the joints, bound together by sinews and tendons; Ibn Zayd takes it to mean strength. Al-Tabari and Ibn 'Atiyya support their choice with lines of Arabic poetry. Mujahid is also reported to have meant the place where waste leaves the body, a sense mentioned by al-Sam'ani and al-Baghawi without making it the primary meaning.

As for "We would replace them with their likes", the commentators agree it means destroying them and bringing others in their place. Al-Tabari and Ibn Kathir understand other people of the same kind, while in another narration Ibn Abbas speaks of changing them into uglier forms, and Ibn Kathir sees in the verse a proof of resurrection. Al-Zamakhshari holds that the particle should be "in" rather than "idha", a point that al-Razi and Abu Hayyan answer by noting that "idha" signals that the event is certain to occur.

The verse belongs to a passage condemning those who prefer the fleeting life and neglect the heavy Day, which Ibn Kathir and al-Baghawi identify as the Day of Resurrection. On "This is a reminder", al-Tabari takes it as the surah, while Ibn 'Atiyya considers it may refer to the verse, the surah or the whole law. Ibn Juzayy holds that "whoever wills" is not a free choice but an exhortation and a warning, and Ibn Kathir notes that human will remains subject to God's will.

This verse says that this surah is a reminder and an admonition, and that whoever wills may take a path to his Lord. Most commentators understand the word sabil as a means of drawing near to God through obedience: al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, al-Baghawi and al-Qurtubi take it as the way of obedience, while al-Zamakhshari and Abu Hayyan speak of drawing near to God and seeking nearness through obedience. Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi add that this path leads to reward or to Paradise.

As for the word "this", al-Tabari, Ibn Atiyya and Ibn Kathir take it as referring to the surah. Ibn Atiyya allows that it may refer to the verse itself or to the whole Law, and al-Mawardi also considers that it may refer to the human creation itself.

The main disagreement concerns the end of the verse, "and you do not will except that God wills." Ibn Kathir and the Sunni commentators read it as affirming that no one can guide himself without divine will, and Abu Hayyan explains that this denies man the power to originate his intentions while allowing acquisition. Ibn Juzayy and al-Alusi note that al-Zamakhshari understands it as God compelling people, an interpretation the Sunnis reject. The readings also differ between the third-person plural, followed by Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr, and the second person used by the other readers.

The commentators agree that guidance belongs to God alone, who guides whom He wills.

This verse closes the passage by affirming that a person's will takes effect only when God wills it, and that no one can take a path to his Lord except with God's permission. Al-Tabari, Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and al-Baghawi explain that people can reach obedience only if God grants it to them, since the matter belongs to Him alone. Ibn Kathir adds that no one can guide himself, and that God guides whom He wills and misguides whom He wills. The commentators agree that mercy in the phrase (He admits whom He wills into His mercy) means Paradise or faith, and that the wrongdoers, meaning the polytheists, will face a painful punishment. Ibn Kathir, Ibn al-Jawzi and Abu Hayyan note that the reciters differ on the verb (tashā'ūn): Ibn Kathir and Abu 'Amr read it with the ya, while the others read it with the ta.

The sharpest disagreement concerns human will. Al-Tabari, al-Sam'ani, al-Nasafi and Ibn Juzayy hold that people have a will subordinate to God's, which Sunni scholars call acquisition (kasb). Al-Zamakhshari reads the verse as meaning that God compels people to obey, a reading that Ibn al-Munayyir, Abu al-Su'ud and al-Alusi reject or qualify. Ibn 'Ashur sees the verse as a subtle statement that joins human and divine will without opposing them. Al-Razi notes that the end of the surah expresses absolute monotheism.

On grammar, al-Tabari, Ibn 'Atiyya and Ibn al-Jawzi explain that (al-zalimin) is in the accusative by an implied verb that the phrase (a'adda lahum) clarifies, and that the nominative reading, attributed to Ibn al-Zubayr and Aban ibn 'Uthman, is also accepted.

This part of the verse says that God admits into His mercy whom He wills, and that He has prepared a painful punishment for the wrongdoers. Most commentators take mercy to mean Paradise: al-Tabari says it is Paradise granted to the one who repents until death, Ibn Kathir and al-Jalalayn take it to mean the believers, while al-Sam'ani gives Paradise as the primary meaning and notes the view that it means Islam, preferring the first because the verse goes on to speak of the Fire. As for the wrongdoers, al-Tabari, al-Baghawi and al-Jalalayn identify them as the polytheists or disbelievers, al-Tabari specifying those who die in their shirk. The commentators agree that the verse shows entry into mercy lies in God's will, which takes precedence over the human will mentioned just before. Al-Razi draws from this that entry into Paradise comes through God's grace rather than strict merit. Al-Zamakhshari reads God's will as compulsion, a view rejected by al-Tabari, while Ibn al-Jawzi, citing the Sunni position, speaks of human acquisition (kasb) of the act. Grammatically, al-Zamakhshari, Ibn Atiyya and al-Razi explain that the word for wrongdoers is in the accusative under an implied verb, 'He punishes', while the reading of Aban ibn Uthman in the nominative is considered less preferable by most. All agree on the general meaning: a promise to believers and a warning to wrongdoers.
